transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-12
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Rajiv Menon (Haven Infra), Sofia Ruiz (Haven ML), Ethan Cole (Haven Security), Nina Park (Haven Procurement)

Auto Summary (auto): quick sync to align on air-gapped transfer, license activation, and perf bench plan

Topics: artifact delivery, licensing, drivers, quant benchmarking, kv warmup, batching

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — we have Rajiv, Sofia, Ethan, Nina — you there?
[00:10] Rajiv Menon: Yep, here. Sorry slight echo on my side.
[00:14] Liam O'Connor: Hi all, Liam from Redwood. We'll jump into the transfer and then benchmarking.
[00:18] Sofia Ruiz: Great, we've been looking at on-prem options, um, and want to validate the int4/int8 tradeoffs for our customer-facing latency constraints.
[00:26] Ethan Cole: From security we need to lock down the signing and KMS flow — airgapped means no outbound calls so how do we activate licenses?
[00:36] Maya: Exactly — we'll outline the offline licensing handshake we use: signed activation blob, time-limited token wrapped with customer's public key, plus checksum and attestation file. We'll share the checklist.
[00:48] Rajiv: For transport we will be doing physical media handoff — drives go to our secure staging. Need to confirm checksum and signature verification steps so we can automate locally.
[00:58] Liam: We'll provide a small verification CLI that validates bundle signature and SHA-256 checksums, plus an offline verifier that we can run in the staging network. It outputs a signed attest token you can store.
[01:12] Sofia: Can you also confirm the bundle contents? Model artifacts, runtime, drivers, kernel modules?
[01:18] Maya: Yes — bundle = model weights (quantized variants), runtime docker images (or OCI tarball), kernel module tar (for NV/AMD), license blob, checksums, and a manifest. We sign the manifest with Redwood's offline signing key.
[01:34] Nina Park: Procurement question — what does license activation look like for airgapped? Do we need a signed physical dongle?
[01:42] Maya: No dongle. The flow we use: we generate an offline activation package tied to your HSM-wrapped customer key; you run the verifier, it returns a local activation token. If HSM required, we can wrap with your public HSM key.
[01:58] Ethan: Clarify HSM: we want to avoid keys leaving our network; so we need a process where Redwood provides signed artifacts but the activation only completes once our HSM signs the final ack.
[02:10] Liam: That's supported. We support customer-side wrapping/unwrapping steps: Redwood supplies the signed license, you use on-prem KMS/HSM to unwrap and generate the final activation. We'll include an example with PKCS#11 calls.
[02:24] Rajiv: Cool. On the GPU side, our cluster is a mixed fleet: A100s and some Instinct MI250s. Driver compatibility is a big concern — ROCm vs CUDA.
[02:36] Liam: Right, for MI250 we rely on ROCm kernels. Our runtime chooses kernels at startup based on GPU capability. Caveat: some attention/kernels are optimized more heavily for CUDA right now; ROCm parity is improving but we should test.
[02:50] Sofia: Do you provide prebuilt kernel blobs for ROCm or do we compile?
[02:54] Liam: We provide prebuilt ROCm-compatible kernels for supported OS versions. If your distro or kernel is older, we have build scripts. We'll list supported driver versions in the bundle manifest.
[03:06] Rajiv: What about firmware/driver pins? We can't upgrade firmware easily.
[03:10] Liam: We'll include a compatibility matrix. If a specific kernel needs newer firmware we call it out. For those nodes we can run the CPU fallback or a different quant profile.
[03:20] Sofia: Let's talk quantization. We care about latency p50/p95 and worst-case p99. Our UX SLO is p95 < 120ms for 512-token prompts.
[03:30] Liam: Understood. In our experience int8 gives strong latency with high throughput; int4 has better memory but can regress per-token quality and sometimes increases tail latency due to less stable kernel behavior on some GPUs. We recommend running a small sweep: fp16, int8, int4 with your 3 prompt sets.
[03:52] Speaker 1: I think we saw, um, in other tests — int4 occasionally cause token collapse on long context, so need evals.
[04:02] Maya: Good note. The planned microbenchmarks will capture quality metrics (perplexity/acceptance) as well as latencies. Liam will run latency and KV warmup traces.
[04:14] Rajiv: How does KV cache warmup look in an airgapped staging environment? We can't prepopulate caches from production.
[04:22] Liam: We have two options: generate synthetic prefix traces to warm caches during warm-up window, or ship a small set of real prompt history (anonymized) that you load once. The runtime supports preloading KV blobs as part of the bundle install.
[04:38] Sofia: If we preload, does eviction policy differ with quantized weights?
[04:44] Liam: Eviction is orthogonal to quantization — it depends on KV capacity and sequence length. But quantization can change memory pressure, so we recommend adjusting KV retention length when moving from fp16 to int8/int4. We'll share heuristics.
[04:58] Ethan: On batching — our primary concern is tail latency for interactive agents. We want batching to improve throughput but not spike p99.
[05:08] Liam: Batching window tuning: small windows (2–6ms) give modest batching but keep tail low. For higher throughput offline workloads you increase the window. Also continuous batching with dynamic cutoffs will lower cost while honoring latency SLOs. We can ship configs tuned per node type.
[05:26] Sofia: Any auto-fallback if a node is slow? We want graceful degradation not errors.
[05:30] Liam: Yes — runtime has routing policies: prefer low-latency pool, fall back to higher-latency pool (dedicated-downgrade), or to hosted fallback if configured. For airgapped we can't fallback to hosted, so we recommend overprovisioning a small buffer pool.
[05:46] Rajiv: For our initial pilot we want to target 200 req/s with 512 tokens median; what's a safe cluster size estimate?
[05:54] Liam: Quick rule of thumb: A100 80GB with int8 and 512 tokens ~180–220 rps depending on batching. We'll provide capacity estimates after we run benchmarks with your prompt mix.
[06:08] Maya: To set expectations: we'll do a two-phase bench — microbench locally to iterate quant knobs, then staging end-to-end with transfer, install, and KV preload.
[06:18] Nina Park: Procurement note — we need an acceptance test and a PSA for the handoff. What does success look like?
[06:24] Maya: Success = bundle verified and installed, license activated offline, p95 latency < 120ms on your representative set, and a passing security checklist. We'll put that in the test plan.
[06:36] Sofia: Can you walk through the sample benchmark outputs — what's included in the logs?
[06:40] Liam: We'll produce per-request latency histograms, token throughput, GPU utilization, KV hit/miss traces, and model output diffs vs baseline. We'll also include raw perf counters.
[06:52] Rajiv: How big are the bundles typically? Models + runtime + drivers — any rough sizes?
[06:56] Liam: For a large LLM with int8 and cache priming assets, expect 40–200GB depending on model size; drivers and runtimes are small relative. We'll provide exact sizes per model.
[07:06] Sofia: About signing: if I verify signature and checksum locally, do we get an attestation file to include in audit logs?
[07:12] Maya: Yes, the verifier emits an attest.json (or text file) that contains bundle digest, verification status, signer fingerprint, and timestamp. That file is included in the audit trail.
[07:24] Ethan: Does Redwood support offline rotation of signing keys? We may require rotating keys frequently and re-verifying bundles on every rotation.
[07:30] Liam: Supported. Rotation flow: you provide a new public key, we re-sign a new manifest and issuance; we can automate reissue if you provide an API or do manual re-signing for stricter controls.
[07:42] Rajiv: Any gotchas around kernel modules and RMM or CUDA versions?
[07:48] Liam: Kernel module ABI changes can break modules — if your kernel version is nonstandard we recommend building at the site. We provide a build container and reproducible build steps.
[07:58] Sofia: For the bench script — can we include long-context failure cases to watch for kv eviction and token collapse?
[08:04] Liam: Absolutely, include long-tail traces. We'll report token stability metrics and divergence vs fp16 baseline.
[08:12] Speaker 2: There's also the thing about power limits — some nodes default to low power mode which kills perf.
[08:18] Rajiv: Yep we had a node with power capping accidentally set; we'll ensure BIOS settings are in the checker list.
[08:24] Maya: We'll include a preflight checklist (BIOS, driver, firmware, kernel, open ports for installer — even though it's airgapped there are a few ephemeral ports internally).
[08:36] Nina Park: And logistics — we need the exact md5/sha values ahead of shipping to match on arrival.
[08:42] Liam: We'll provide SHA-256 and PGP signature. We'll also provide an encrypted manifest for the transport team if needed.
[08:50] Sofia: When do you need the prompt sets?
[08:52] Maya: ASAP — earlier the better. If we get them by 10/15 we can run microbench before the on-site window.
[08:58] Rajiv: We'll aim for 10/16 for topology and 10/15 for prompts.
[09:04] Liam: Okay next, small note on logging and retention — audit logs for license activation are stored locally in the attestation store; we support exporting to your SIEM via file drop or syslog.
[09:16] Ethan: Confirm that logs do not include user data from prompts, we need PII-redaction controls.
[09:22] Liam: By default logs contain metadata and digests; content redaction is configurable. We'll share the config options.
[09:28] Maya: To wrap up, quick recap and owners. Action items spelled out in the meeting notes.
[09:36] Sofia: Sounds good. Anything else?
[09:38] Rajiv: No, thanks.
[09:40] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the signed-bundle checklist and schedule the bench run.

End of transcript.
